mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Ahriman ‌place ​evil, destruction, ​lies ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Ahriman ‌appears in ​zoroastrian ‌tradition ​as evil, ​destruction, ​lies. The ​name's ​meaning, ‌"Evil spirit, ​destructive ‌mind", ​shapes the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Ahriman ​in ‌ritual, text, ​and ​iconography, ensuring ‌the ​name ​survived into ‌the ​modern scholarly ‌record.

​The ​myths of ​Ahriman ​survive in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, ​and later ‌retellings. ​Each ​version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ​— poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The ‌PuniCodex entry ​does ​not ​privilege a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the ‌attestations so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Ahriman ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming 𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 ‌𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult ​remains ​tied to ​evil ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Ahriman** ​(*ahriman*) — ‌Evil, Destruction, ‌Lies ​· Evil ​spirit, ​destructive mind ​— belongs ​to ‌the Zoroastrian ​tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Evil, ‌Destruction, Lies". ​The name ​means ​"Evil spirit, ​destructive ​mind"[^1].

**Ahriman** ‌is the ​Evil ‌Spirit of ​Zoroastrianism ‌— Avestan ​*Aŋra Mainyu*, ‌'destructive ​mind' — ‌the ​adversary of ​the wise ‌lord ‌Ohrmazd. He ‌is ​not a ​rival god ‌but ​the Lie ​made ‌willful: choice ​turned against ​creation. ‌The tradition ​is ‌emphatic that ​he creates ​nothing, ​can only ​corrupt, ‌and is ‌destined to ​lose.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ​the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Ahriman** ‌and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/ahriman/). The ​displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*ahriman* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Avestan ​as **𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 ​𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎**. ​Etymologically ​it means ‌"Evil ​spirit, ​destructive mind"[^1].

‌The ​canonical ‌spelling ​**Ahriman** matches ‌the ​conventional ​scholarly romanization. ​The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*ahriman* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so ​no ‌lost diacritics ​or ‌encoding ​transition is ​claimed. ‌The ‌editorial work ‌is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed ​reference ​spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and ​provenance, ‌and keep ​the ‌original ​evidence visible. ​The ​displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the ‌displayed form ‌itself.

meditation.body:
Ahriman ​is the ‌rarest thing ‌in mythology: ​a god ​of ​evil whom ​his own ​tradition insists ‌is ​not a ​god. The ‌Gāthās will ​not let ‌him ​be a ‌second creator ​or an ​equal power; ​they ​make him ​a choice ‌— the ​will ‌that looked ​on truth ‌and chose ​otherwise. What ‌later ​centuries built ‌into a ​towering demon-king ​began ‌as something ‌more unsettling: ‌the recognition ​that evil ​needs ‌no substance, ​only a ​decision, and ‌that the ​decision ​is available ‌to everyone, ​always.

This ‌is ​why Zoroastrian ​eschatology is ​so strange ​to readers ‌raised ‌on Norse ​or Christian ‌endings. There ​is no ​last ‌battle whose ‌outcome is ‌uncertain, no ‌twilight ​in which ‌evil wins ​the field. ​Ahriman's defeat ​is ‌announced at ​his first ​appearance; his ​entire ‌mythology is ​a working-out ​of a ​foregone conclusion ‌— ​which means ‌the drama ​was never ‌really about ​him. ‌It is ‌about us, ​standing where ​he ​stood, asked ​the question ‌he was ‌asked, and ​answering.[^1]
